articles.title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds
articles.summary: Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. articles.body: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. The risk relates to declining demand for fossil fuel cargoes which could reduce the need for vessels such as LNG carriers. It is separate but related to the risks faced by all shipowners as they manage the energy transition that will also take place within international shipping, whether driven by IMO regulation adopted this December, or postponed global regulation accompanied by a patchwork of regional regulation. The new report finds that the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is the most credible route to the single global rulebook that the shipping industry, including the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has called for. A weaker, technical-only outcome at the IMO would leave the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) alongside the IMO fuel standard, as well as incentivising additions to other unilateral carbon pricing such as those already started in Africa – which is the regional patchwork UGS warns against. Greece owns about a fifth of the world fleet, roughly 5,800 ships and 460 million deadweight tonnes (dwt). Greek shipowners collectively have particularly leading market shares in ownership of the oil tankers, LNG carriers and bulk carriers that move fossil fuels, making them more exposed to transition risks than any other nation. Owners cannot change demand for fossil fuel cargoes, but they can influence how shipping is regulated. The report finds that the NZF would give them a predictable timetable, more compliance options and a managed exit from LNG exposure, reducing the risk of stranded assets. Dr Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy and Transport at UCL Energy Insitute and co-director of the Shipping and Oceans Research Group said “Greek owners already face one transition they cannot control, which is related to changes in the demand for the cargoes their ships carry. Supporting the NZF, the only adoptable architecture on the table at MEPC 85, is a chance to make the second one, in how shipping’s own energy transition is regulated, predictable, lower burden, less complicated and more supportive of a mix of decarbonisation strategies and pathways.” The report, Real economy consequences for Greece from success or failure of the Net-Zero Framework, is published ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 (23 to 27 November) and MEPC 85, which opens on 30 November. At MEPC 84, NZF-like options drew more than twice the support of technical-only alternatives. Earlier this week, UGS President Melina Travlos urged IMO member states to deliver a regulation that is “pragmatic, proportionate and implementable”, and questioned whether the EU is putting its regional measures, and the revenues they generate, ahead of a global deal. The report draws a similar concern about the risk of regulatory fragmentation, particularly how this could disadvantage smaller shipping companies with less capacity and flexibility to manage the administrative burden and timing of shipping’s energy transition. The report finds there is no alternative architecture to NZF that has anywhere close to the levels of support for adoption and efforts that do not support NZF are only increasing risks of stalemate and fragmentation. The European Commission’s commitment to avoid double payment depends on a global carbon price being adopted, so without one, the EU ETS would stay in force on top of the IMO standard. Demetres Karavellas, CEO of WWF Greece said “As climate impacts intensify, shipping must play its part in the transition to net-zero. The IMO Net-Zero Framework is the only credible global pathway to decarbonise the sector while providing the certainty businesses need to invest. This report shows that Greece, as the world’s leading shipping nation, has more to lose from delay than almost anyone else. Opposing the NZF will not stop the transition. It will only increase uncertainty and expose Greek shipping to greater risk. Greece has an opportunity to help shape a global framework rather than face a more fragmented and disruptive transition later.” The report concludes that failure to adopt the NZF, or a delay of more than a year, would weaken the IMO as global regulator, accelerate regional regulation and force a steeper decarbonisation pathway later. The report urges shipowners to engage constructively in developing the NZF and its guidelines, as the only viable, truly global framework. articles.title: Dry Bulk Market: Kamsarmax Rebounds, Soybeans Set Records
articles.summary: While the larger Capesize ship class continues to act as a benchmark for the broader dry bulk market, smaller sizes have shown significant diversion over the past few days. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv commented that “the dry bulk market continues to demonstrate contrasting dynamics across the...
articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Kamsarmax Rebounds, Soybeans Set Records in Hellenic Shipping News 20/11/2026 W hile the larger Capesize ship class continues to act as a benchmark for the broader dry bulk market, smaller sizes have shown significant diversion over the past few days. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Xclusiv commented that “the dry bulk market continues to demonstrate contrasting dynamics across the Kamsarmax and Ultramax segments, although the considerable earnings differential observed in late October has narrowed during the first half of November. According to Baltic Exchange data, average Kamsarmax earnings (P5TC) increased by 5.7% week-on-week, reaching USD 19,063/day on 13 November, compared with USD 16,999/day at the end of October. Meanwhile, Ultramax earnings (S11TC) stood at USD 23,203/day, recording a more modest weekly increase of 1.1%. Consequently, the earnings differential between the two segments has narrowed from USD 6,570/day on 30 October to approximately USD 4,140/day, reflecting an improvement in Kamsarmax market conditions”. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker According to Xclusiv, “despite this recent recovery, Kamsarmax earnings remain 11.2% below their end-September levels, highlighting the persistent pressure facing the segment. The divergence between the two vessel classes continues to reflect differences in cargo exposure, regional tonnage availability and trading flexibility. Kamsarmax vessels remain particularly dependent on coal and grain movements, while Ultramaxes benefit from a more diversified cargo base, including minor bulks, fertilizers, steel products and agricultural commodities. Their onboard cranes also provide greater flexibility in serving smaller ports and terminals with limited infrastructure”. “Against this backdrop, developments in the Brazilian soybean trade offer an encouraging perspective for dry bulk demand. According to market data, Brazil exported a record 108.4 million tonnes of soybeans during January–October 2026, representing a 7.9% increase year-on-year. Remarkably, shipments during these ten months have already exceeded the entire 2025 volume by approximately 600,000 tonnes. Second-quarter exports reached 44.9 million tonnes, up 10.3% year-on-year, while third-quarter volumes increased by 8.1% to 29.7 million tonnes”, the shipbroker said. Meanwhile, “these developments are particularly relevant for the Panamax/Kamsarmax and Supramax/Ultramax segments, which play an important role in agricultural commodity transportation. With China remaining the principal destination for Brazilian soybeans, continued growth in exports could generate additional tonne-mile demand, especially as long-haul Brazil–Asia shipments absorb vessel capacity for extended periods. Nevertheless, the seasonal distribution of Brazilian exports remains an important consideration. October shipments declined by almost 14% compared with September, reflecting the gradual winding down of the previous harvest season. Therefore, although annual export volumes have reached record levels, their immediate contribution to freight market strength may remain uneven, depending on shipment timing and available tonnage”, Xclusiv noted. Source: Xclusiv shipbroker The shipbroker added that “looking further ahead, the outlook remains constructive. The USDA projects Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean production at 186 million tonnes, with exports expected to reach 118 million tonnes. If realised, these volumes could provide further support to dry bulk employment during the upcoming export season, particularly across long-haul routes towards Asia. In the near term, winter coal demand and North American grain shipments could also contribute to improving Kamsarmax employment. However, stronger electricity consumption does not necessarily translate into higher seaborne coal imports, particularly when inventories remain sufficient or domestic production covers additional requirements”. Xclusiv concluded that “overall, while the recent narrowing of the Kamsarmax–Ultramax earnings gap suggests some rebalancing between the segments, sustained recovery will depend on stronger cargo volumes absorbing available vessel supply. Record Brazilian soybean exports provide a positive underlying demand signal, but regional tonnage distribution, seasonal trade patterns and actual tonne-mile growth will remain decisive in determining freight market direction”. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Asian Vessel Availability Tightens Despite Softer Freight in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 20/11/2026 C apesize and Panamax led the weekly freight gains, with the BCI rising 8.6% and the BPI 5.7%, compared with more modest increases of 1.2% for Supramax and 2.3% for Handysize. The improvement was largely concentrated on Atlantic routes, particularly for the larger vessel segments. However, forward vessel availability as of 16 November points to a different pattern across regions and vessel sizes. While C5 West Australia–China retained a surplus of 29 vessels against expected cargoes by day 15 and P6 Singapore–Atlantic was broadly balanced by day 30, Asian Supramax and Handysize routes showed tighter conditions. On S8/S10, expected cargoes exceeded available vessels by 36 over the next 10 days, compared with 19 a week earlier, while the shortfall on HS7 North China widened from 36 to 43 vessels. Despite this tightening, Asian Supramax spot rates continued to decline, indicating that the stronger forward cargo demand relative to available tonnage has not yet been reflected in freight earnings. Figure 1: Supramax S8/S10 Asia and Handysize HS7 North China: cumulative available ships (excluding waiting vessels) vs expected cargoes, day by day from the 16 November 2026 snapshot to 26 November. Shaded band = range from excluding laden and waiting ships (bottom) to all ships including waiting (top). Exact route values (Source: Signal Ocean). FORWARD VESSEL AVAILABILITY | WHAT CHANGED Between the 9 and 16 November snapshots, ten of 14 routes tightened, three loosened and one was unchanged; horizons differ by route, from 10 to 40 days. The largest moves were on C3 Brazil–China (deficit about 48 → 73 by day 40), S8/S10 Asia (19 → 36 by day 10), HS1/HS2 Continent (surplus 40 → 11 by day 15) and S5 West Africa (surplus 23 → 53 by day 20). Table 1: Cumulative available ships (excluding waiting vessels) minus expected cargoes at the route-specific horizon. Negative values indicate a conditional deficit. Signal rule, applied in order: (1) move of 3 ships or less, or under 2.5% of 16 November expected cargoes = Unchanged; (2) under 10% = Slightly tighter/looser; (3) 10% or more = Tighter/Looser. A fall in the balance = tighter (Source: Signal Ocean; snapshots 9 and 16 November 2026). FREIGHT MARKET OVERVIEW Table 2: Global ballasters (empty ships heading to load). The report compares fixed 9 and 16 November counts. (Source: Signal Ocean). KEY TAKEAWAY During the week ending November 13, the Baltic Dry Index (BDI) climbed to 2,980, supported by gains across all four vessel classes, led by Capesize and Panamax ships on Atlantic routes. However, forward data from November 16 indicated a shifting market dynamic: while Capesize and Panamax routes remained balanced or in oversupply, Asian Supramax and Handysize sectors faced vessel shortages that had not yet been reflected in their spot rates. CAPESIZE Freight. The BCI closed the week at 4,719 on 13 November, up 375 points, and eased 161 points to 4,558 on Monday 16 November. Over the week to 16 November, C8 transatlantic rose $3,781/day to $47,750/day and C9 fronthaul rose $1,488/day to $74,544/day, the highest-earning route. C14 China–Brazil fell $2,382/day to $37,827/day. C3 Brazil–China fell $1.48/t to $35.04/t, while C5 West Australia–China was flat at $13.81/t, which narrowed the C3–C5 spread to $21.23/t from $22.72/t. Figure 2: Capesize route rates and weekly change, 16 November vs 9 November 2026 assessments (Source: Baltic Exchange/Signal Ocean). Figure 3: Capesize ballasters by region, 9 and 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). Figure 4: Capesize available ships (excluding waiting vessels) vs expected cargoes, C3 (40-day horizon) and C5 (15-day horizon), 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). The C3 Brazil–China rate fell over the week even though the 16 November snapshot showed an approximately 73-ship deficit at the 40-day horizon. C5, on a 15-day horizon, showed a 29-ship surplus. Global ballasters fell from 607 to 595, led by the South Atlantic (79 to 56). PANAMAX Freight. The BPI rose 115 points to 2,118. The Atlantic led: P1A transatlantic rose $2,609/day to $18,586/day and P2A fronthaul rose $1,486/day to $25,720/day, the highest-earning route. P6 rose $1,137/day to $18,224/day and P5 rose $317/day to $18,989/day, while P3A Pacific fell $422/day to $20,084/day. Grain routes P7 and P8 edged up to $68.75/t and $52.79/t. Figure 5: Panamax route rates and weekly change, 13 November vs 6 November 2026 (Source: Baltic Exchange/Signal Ocean). Figure 6: Panamax ballasters by region, 9 and 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). Figure 7: Panamax available ships (excluding waiting vessels) vs expected cargoes: P1/P2/P7 and P3 (20 days), P5 (10 days), P6 (30 days), 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). The P5TC was still 12.9% below its level a month earlier. Far East/North Pacific ballasters rose from 200 to 249, while P5 Indonesia–China showed a deficit of about 55 ships by day 10 and P1/P2/P7 about 11 by day 18; P6 was level at day 30. A larger regional ballast pool does not translate directly into ships eligible for a specific route and loading window. SUPRAMAX Freight. The BSI rose 21 points to 1,836. Supramax gains were concentrated in the Atlantic: S4A US Gulf rose $7,351/day to $37,107/day and S1C $2,853/day to $32,325/day. Asian and Indian Ocean routes fell: S2 −$1,076/day, S8 −$792/day, S10 −$725/day and S15 −$1,111/day; the Asia index (S3TC_63) lost $912/day to $22,130/day. Figure 8: Supramax route rates and weekly change, 13 November vs 6 November 2026 (Source: Baltic Exchange/Signal Ocean). Figure 9: Supramax ballasters by region, 9 and 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). Figure 10: Supramax available ships vs expected cargoes: S4A/S1C, S4B and S5 (20 days), S8/S10 (10 days), 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). On S8/S10, the forward balance and the rate moves pointed in opposite directions. S5 West Africa showed a surplus of about 53 ships by day 20, so the Supramax picture was uneven across basins. Ballasters fell from 723 to 679, with Australasia down from 202 to 171 and the Indian Ocean/South Africa from 153 to 133. HANDYSIZE Freight. The BHSI rose 24 points to 1,047. HS4 US Gulf led, up $1,921/day to $21,314/day; HS3 South Atlantic rose $812/day to $29,606/day, the highest-earning route. In Asia, HS7 rose $150/day to $19,100/day, HS5 rose $131/day, and HS6 rose $25/day. Figure 11: Handysize route rates and weekly change, 13 November vs 6 November 2026 (Source: Baltic Exchange/Signal Ocean). Figure 12: Handysize ballasters by region, 9 and 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). Figure 13: Handysize available ships vs expected cargoes: HS1/HS2 and HS5 (15 days), HS6 (20 days), HS7 (10 days), 16 November 2026 (Source: Signal Ocean). The BHSI set a new 52-week high. HS7 North China showed a deficit of about 43 ships by day 10 while its rate rose only modestly; HS5 Southeast Asia and HS6 North China showed surpluses of about 40 and 14 ships, so the Asian picture was not uniformly tight. Ballasters fell from 677 to 664, with the North Atlantic down from 203 to 174. Source: By Maria Bertzletou, Signal Group, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/weekly-market-monitor/weekly-dry-market-monitor-week-46-2026 Tops 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping
articles.summary: There is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, ...
articles.body: Get your data in order and set a course for greener shipping in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 T here is cause for optimism in the shipping sector, and we are seeing more and more initiatives aimed at making shipping greener. Shipowners are now far more willing to reduce emissions from ships than they were just a few years ago. That said, we must also acknowledge that the shipping industry has a data problem, which means shipowners are not getting the insights needed to accelerate the green transition. In the coming weeks alone, there are two events worth keeping an eye on. From 23 to 27 November, the IMO’s working group known as ISWG-GHG 23 will continue its discussions on a global Net-Zero Framework – that is, proposals for common, global climate rules designed to steer the shipping industry towards net-zero emissions by 2050. A few days later, from 30 November to 3 December, the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) will convene for MEPC 85, with emissions, energy efficiency and environmental protection, amongst other topics, on the agenda. There remains disagreement over the way forward, but the work being done within the IMO, amongst others, demonstrates a willingness to find common solutions. I sense the same willingness when I speak to shipping companies and other industry stakeholders. Compared with just three years ago, there is far greater interest in concrete climate action. René Bredmose Christensen, Green Instruments However, although progress is being made, the shipping industry still has a data problem. We still know too little about the emissions of individual ships and how they can reduce their fuel consumption. Far too many people still rely on calculations that are, at best, uncertain and, at worst, misleading. Shipowners cannot navigate between new requirements and regulations blindfolded. They need valid data to set the right course. Calculations and standard values do not reveal how engines perform during operation or how high emissions really are. In the coming years, shipping companies will have to deal with the use of multiple fuels, technologies and types of emissions. How do they assess emissions from different fuels whilst at sea? How do they demonstrate that an investment reduces emissions? And how do they determine the engine settings that deliver the lowest fuel consumption? Here, real-time measurements are a crucial tool – for documentation, compliance with requirements and day-to-day decision-making. The new five-year partnership between the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Equinor is a strong example of how the green transition requires joint efforts and practical trials. They will collaborate on areas including alternative fuels, energy efficiency and CO₂ management. Their emphasis on documentation and verification is entirely appropriate. After all, shipowners and organisations can only derive the full benefit from such initiatives if they have access to valid data. I therefore hope that they will involve experts in emissions measurement to a greater extent at an early stage of the process. This increases the likelihood that we can actually learn from each other’s experiences. At the same time, shipowners can take advantage of some straightforward opportunities. Linking real-time measurements to the engines’ operational data would enable shipping companies to identify which operating conditions increase fuel consumption and emissions. However, without the necessary equipment on board, these opportunities are easily overlooked. With valid data, shipping companies can act immediately to reduce costs and cut emissions. I hope that the IMO meetings will bring the shipping industry closer to achieving common climate regulations. However, these regulations cannot stand alone. The green course must be set collectively and guided by what we can measure and document. Source: By Rene B. Christensen, CEO, Green Instruments Tops 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions
articles.summary: Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating...
articles.body: Smart Sea urges shipowners to tackle ageing infrastructure before investing in new digital solutions in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Shipowners risk undermining their digitalisation efforts by investing in new technology while continuing to operate outdated and potentially vulnerable IT systems, according to maritime technology consultancy SmartSea. Recent fleet assessments by the company have identified vessels still running unsupported operating systems, including Windows 7, raising concerns over cybersecurity, system reliability and the ability to integrate modern digital applications. Kris Vedat, CEO of Smart Sea, warns that too many operators are prioritising new software and connectivity over the infrastructure needed to support them. “We’re still finding vessels running operating systems that have been unsupported for years,” said Mr Vedat. “That’s a cybersecurity risk and a major obstacle to digitalisation. There’s little point investing in sophisticated technology if the underlying systems aren’t fit for purpose.” Mr Vedat believes the industry needs to move away from short-term technology fixes towards a more co-ordinated approach that includes infrastructure assessments, standardised processes and phased implementation. “Crew training is essential, but it’s only part of the solution. Digital transformation isn’t about buying more software. It’s about making sure the systems, processes and people are ready to make it work,” he explained. The SmartSea CEO also cautions against focusing too heavily on short-term savings. Cheaper satellite connectivity, for example, can quickly become a false economy if poor integration, unreliable data flows or security weaknesses create additional operational costs. Kris Vedat, CEO, SmartSea Mr Vedat said: “Saving money upfront means very little if it creates bigger problems down the line. Technology investments should be judged on the operational value they deliver, not simply the immediate cost savings.” The lack of consistent technical standards across shipping adds to the challenge, particularly for third-party ship managers inheriting vessels with ageing IT and operational technology. Smart Sea believes clearer minimum standards would help improve cybersecurity and support more effective fleet-wide digitalisation. Mr Vedat believes addressing these technical and commercial barriers is essential if shipping is to realise the full potential of digitalisation, automation and decarbonisation technologies. He added: “Shipping doesn’t have a shortage of technology. The challenge is making it work effectively. Operators need to stop chasing quick fixes and focus on getting the foundations right. Otherwise, they risk spending more on technology without seeing the benefits.” Source: Smart Sea 2026-11-20 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Drewry: Asia-Europe capacity returns via Suez – but security concerns remain in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 Drewry’s Red Sea Diversion Tracker delivers timely intelligence to shippers, carriers, ports and other stakeholders on the evolving structure of carrier networks. This tracker page is updated fortnightly (every other Tuesday). During the week ended 15 Nov, a total of 57 containerships transited the Suez Canal (in either direction), up 73% when compared with the number in the same week of 2025, with 60% of Asia-Europe capacity now using the Suez route again. There have now been 7 weeks with more than 50 Suez transits a week, indicating a continued momentum in the return of containerships from the Cape of Good Hope route to the Suez route. The average number of transits via Suez was 54 in the latest 3 weeks, about the same as in the previous three weeks. The number of transits around the Cape of Good Hope continued to decline during the week ended 15 Nov, with only 126 transits, the lowest weekly total since January 2026. 17 NOV: SECURITY WATCH Material deterioration in Bab al-Mandeb security situation: While encouraging to see the steady return of transits via Red Sea and Suez, in recent days there has been a material deterioration in the security situation in the vicinity of Bab al-Mandab with government forces withdrawing from their positions overlooking the Strait. This creates an uncomfortable strategic picture for commercial shipping – returning to the Red Sea just as the Houthis re-establish their position around this important maritime chokepoint. Source: Drewry Container Capacity Insight Improving Red Sea traffic figures should therefore be treated with caution and not extrapolated to set expectations for December and January. articles.body: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 20/11/2026 North America Prompt availability of all three grades is tight in Houston and Bolivar Roads. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is better for deliveries more than a week out. At the Galveston Offshore Lightering Area (GOLA), HSFO availability is normal. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight. VLSFO availability is normal in New Orleans. Prompt HSFO and LSMGO availability is tight in Lake Charles. Bunker demand is subdued in New York. VLSFO and LSMGO can be delivered with lead times of four days. VLSFO availability has improved from last week, when the grade needed over a week to 10 days of notice. Prompt HSFO availability is tight, with recommended lead times of six days. LSMGO availability is normal in Savannah. On the US West Coast, VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight in Los Angeles. Suppliers are recommending LSMGO lead times of over a week to two weeks, up from 5-7 days last week. In Canada, VLSFO and LSMGO can be delivered in Vancouver within four days. In a statement to Iran’s state broadcaster, the paramilitary group said the ships were carrying over 4 million barrels of crude and attempting to traverse the southern section of Hormuz under the protection of the U.S. military. The Associated Press said the Iranian claims could not be immediately verified and U.S. Central Command, which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, did not comment. Tehran has frequently warned ships against transiting Hormuz, a vital waterway for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the start of the U.S.-Israel assault on Iran in late February. Iran has moved to close down the strait, although shipments have begun to improve in recent months, fueling some predictions that global oil supply could soon outstrip demand. Benchmark Brent crude prices have fallen by more than fifth so far this month. However, in a potential sign of the impact of the Iranian attacks, crude shipments through the strait appear to have fallen since the start of November. Data firm Kpler said the number of shipments going through Hormuz have declined to 8.5 million barrels per day, or around half of the prewar levels reached at the beginning of the month. Still, Kpler flagged that shipments could recover over the rest of November. According to media reports, tanker crews have had to employ a ship-to-ship transit procedure to take oil barrels out of the Persian Gulf, a risky process that has sparked a surge in vessel chartering rates. Meanwhile, there have been few indications that the standoff in Hormuz is softening. U.S. President Donald Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, considering fresh intelligence about Tehran’s military capabilities and mounting pressure from Israel to launch an aggressive campaign, The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing U.S. and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions. Trump has not made a final decision, but is assessing Israeli warnings that Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs, the report said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing Washington to join Israel in a four- to seven-day campaign of airstrikes, seeking to capitalize on the U.S. military presence in the region, according to the report. articles.summary: A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: tcly / Shutterstock By Arathy Somasekhar HOUSTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) – A court ruling has jeopardized a license for Sentinel Midstream’s $2.1 billion deepwater crude oil export project off the Texas coast, an environmental group that petitioned the court said this week. The ruling, which took effect on October 30, poses a setback and likely delays for the oil transportation and storage company, which has already started work on the project. It could also impact other pending deepwater port applications. In August, a US appeals court voided a federal record of decision for Sentinel Midstream’s Texas GulfLink project, citing overlap with another deepwater project. An official at Sentinel Midstream said work would continue on the project, characterizing it as “business as usual.” But a source with knowledge of the situation said the company could not continue with the offshore project on the current license. Last year, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD), in its record of decision (ROD), approved Texas GulfLink with conditions and the company received its license in January 2026 . President Donald Trump has pushed for faster project approvals to bolster the US energy industry. Sentinel made a final investment decision in May and began construction. MARAD’s record of decision approving Texas GulfLink’s application violated the Deepwater Port Act’s requirement that only one deepwater port be approved per application area, the 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals said. Texas GulfLink’s application area, when properly designated, would have intersected with Enterprise Products Partners’ Sea Port Oil Terminal (SPOT) deepwater project. Congress has struck a careful balance between promoting and regulating the construction and operation of deepwater ports, the court said, holding that the Deepwater Port Act requires an application area to encompass the entirety of a proposed deepwater port site, including any proposed pipeline. “The Court’s decision is clear: it vacated the record of decision that was the foundation of GulfLink’s license. Now, MARAD has to revoke or suspend that license,” Michael Brown, a counsel for the petitioners, said on Wednesday. Construction of the project cannot continue without a federal deepwater port license, said environmental group Better Brazoria Clean Air and Water in a press release this week. MARAD said it was disappointed with the outcome and continues to pursue all avenues to achieve the President’s vision of American energy dominance. “Sentinel is working with MARAD to discuss its options for moving forward. The company cannot continue with the current license,” a source familiar with the matter said. In comments to Reuters this week, Sentinel said its license has not been suspended or terminated. Texas GulfLink, to be situated about 30 miles off Freeport, Texas, remains on track for a fourth-quarter 2028 operational date, Bruce Heine, a senior vice president at Sentinel, said this week, adding that given the narrow nature and scope of the issue, there are multiple paths to address the statutory concern without disrupting ongoing construction activities or overall project schedule. “It remains business as usual for Texas GulfLink, with site development and improvement activities currently underway at our Jones Creek onshore terminal facility as we prepare to commence tank construction,” Heine said, adding that major long-lead equipment and pipe have been purchased, and key construction contracts executed. However, the company in its motion last month to stay the court mandate said that the Texas GulfLink’s license expressly incorporates the ROD as a compliance standard, adding that voiding the ROD in turn exposed the license to suspension or revocation by MARAD, and prevents construction of offshore components. “At a minimum, the cloud on Texas GulfLink’s regulatory posture will harm Texas GulfLink in the marketplace,” the company said then, adding that “given the uncertainty of its ROD and license, Texas GulfLink will not commence construction of the deepwater port under the current posture, even if the mandate is stayed.” Texas GulfLink plans to petition the Supreme Court, the company said in its motion. It added that there are two other pending deepwater ports under review with application areas similar to Texas GulfLink’s that will likely require redesignation as a result of the panel’s decision, potentially resulting in consequential impacts to those projects as well. If Sentinel is required to resubmit its application, it would have to await a new ROD and license. While it took nearly seven years for Sentinel to secure approvals last time, MARAD has sped up its approval process under US President Donald Trump. It recently issued a deepwater project application license in just 410 days, nearly 3.7 years faster than ?the historical average. The Texas GulfLink project aims to fully load a supertanker with about 2 million barrels of oil per day. The administration in recent weeks also approved deepwater port license applications for Energy Transfer’s ET.N Blue Marlin Offshore Port, an oil export project off the Louisiana coast, and for ST LNG, which aims to ship liquefied natural gas off ?the Texas coast. articles.title: Who calls the shots when it comes to ship finance in Hong Kong?
articles.summary: Tax incentives, Chinese leasing capital and a deep banking network are keeping Hong Kong relevant to global shipping. But the industry’s biggest question is whether deals are genuinely made in the city, or merely booked there. A major containership financing this autumn illustrates both Hong Kong’s reach and its...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Greater China Who calls the shots when it comes to ship finance in Hong Kong? Splash November 20, 2026 0 204 4 minutes read Victor Halder Victor Halder Tax incentives, Chinese leasing capital and a deep banking network are keeping Hong Kong relevant to global shipping. But the industry’s biggest question is whether deals are genuinely made in the city, or merely booked there. A major containership financing this autumn illustrates both Hong Kong’s reach and its limitations. Global Ship Lease’s new $1bn syndicated facility includes Bank of China (Hong Kong) and BOCOM Hong Kong among eight lenders supporting 15 newbuildings. But Bank of America is the bookrunner, and the money comes from a syndicate spanning three continents. A vessel can be ordered in China, owned through another jurisdiction, financed by multiple banks and leased to a charterer thousands of miles away. Where, then, does the financial centre sit? Hong Kong is determined that the answer should increasingly be Hong Kong. The government’s 2026 Policy Address introduced a Finance + Shipping agenda, promising closer integration of ship lending, marine insurance, common-law documentation and arbitration. The aim is to become more than a location for leasing vehicles. The backdrop is an expanding global financing market. Petrofin calculates that the world’s 40 largest shipping banks held $300.6bn in loans at the end of 2025, up 6% year-on-year, while leasing and alternative capital providers are taking an increasingly important role. Hong Kong is hardly starting from nothing. Hong Kong Trade Development Council figures show HK$105bn ($13.5bn) in shipping loans and advances booked locally at the end of June, equivalent to 1.4% of loans for use in Hong Kong. Some overseas-booked loans involving Hong Kong professionals are not captured in that total. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, rejects the idea that finance either originates in Hong Kong or is controlled entirely from Beijing and Shanghai. “Modern ship finance is often originated, structured, syndicated, insured and documented across several centres,” he says. Hong Kong’s opportunity is to assemble those functions around its banks, common-law contracts, capital markets and proximity to mainland Chinese shipping customers. The growth of ship leasing Ship leasing is where policy has delivered the most measurable growth. Since 2020, qualifying ship lessors have enjoyed a zero profits-tax rate, while eligible leasing managers receive an 8.25% rate. Government figures show the number of qualifying leasing enterprises rose from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. But enterprise numbers do not measure loans originated or jobs created. The business has genuine scale. Hong Kong-listed CSSC Shipping, backed by China State Shipbuilding Corporation, had 130 vessels in its leasing portfolio, including 23 under construction, as of June. This year it raised HK$2.338bn in convertible bonds, while its growing fleet business illustrates the links between Chinese yards, capital markets and vessel leasing. Independent firms add another dimension. SeaKapital, established in 2023 by shipowner Sabrina Chao and former Credit Agricole Asia Shipfinance chief Kenneth Lam, aims to connect shipping assets with international investors from its Hong Kong base. However, local incorporation does not automatically mean local control. KC Maritime chairman Gautam Chellaram draws an important distinction between international banks and independent leasing businesses that make financing decisions in the city and major mainland leasing groups whose pricing, credit approvals and portfolio strategy are largely set across the border. “I believe Hong Kong is doing both, depending on which part of the market we consider,” he says. Chellaram sees little clear evidence that tax breaks alone have brought substantial relocations of head offices, investment mandates and senior decision-makers. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. What matters is attracting people with real lending authority, not just low-tax structures. The mainland bridge Angad Banga, chief executive of The Caravel Group, argues that the question should not be reduced to a contest between Hong Kong and the mainland. “Shipping finance is increasingly collaborative rather than concentrated in a single city,” he says. Hong Kong connects global capital and legal expertise to China’s enormous trading and shipbuilding economy. Singapore nevertheless remains a formidable competitor. Its maritime authority identifies more than 20 major banks with ship-finance portfolios, alongside shipping trusts, investment banks and private equity providers. Beyond tax incentives, its concentration of charterers, commodity traders and commercial principals brings lenders physically closer to customers and decisions. New legislation Hong Kong’s concessions are being updated. Legislation introduced in June proposed improved tax treatment of ship acquisition costs for qualifying operating lessors, alongside an elective 15% tax-rate option aimed at reducing compliance complexity for multinational groups subject to international minimum-tax rules. The broader package also targeted physical commodity traders, whose presence could deepen the city’s commercial shipping network. Bjorn Hojgaard, chief executive of Anglo-Eastern, sees scope for expansion, particularly as fleet renewal and decarbonisation demand more capital. “Hong Kong has the banking, capital-markets and advisory depth to play a larger role in ship finance, leasing and green maritime investment than it does today,” he says. Hong Kong’s five-year plan identifies green newbuildings, retrofits and cross-border renminbi settlement as opportunities. But financing the transition means assessing future fuel availability, charter income, technology risk and residual ship values. Chellaram proposes a commercially underwritten first-loss guarantee and co-investment facility for cleaner ships and related infrastructure. Such a scheme would involve more direct risk-sharing than another tax break. Geopolitics Another test is geopolitical. Splash has reported Chinese lessors turning to Maltese flag structures to rebuild financing relationships with European owners as China-related commercial concerns mount. Hong Kong’s separate legal and financial system can facilitate cross-border transactions, but cannot entirely remove the political risks perceived by counterparties. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, describes ship finance and leasing as part of an increasingly integrated mainland-Hong Kong financial system. “This is not a matter of ‘who leads’, but of how the whole system can more effectively serve the maritime economy,” he says. Hext argues the decisive measures should be local underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks, skilled jobs and headquarters, rather than company registrations alone. The territory remains a substantial ship finance centre, not merely a postal address. But the next stage of its revival depends on persuading more financiers not just to sign and book deals in Hong Kong, but to make the decisions there. Photo courtesy ARC Shipping American Roll-On/Roll-Off Carrier Group (ARC) has added another large vehicle carrier to its U.S.-flag fleet, strengthening its ability to transport heavy military equipment and commercial cargo overseas. The 757-foot ARC United (IMO 9505053) joins the fleet under the federal Maritime Security Program (MSP), which maintains commercially operated U.S.-flag ships available to support military sealift requirements during war and national emergencies. The Large Car and Truck Carrier (LCTC) has 13 cargo decks, including five with hoistable sections, and capacity for nearly 8,000 car-equivalent units. Its stern ramp can handle rolling loads of up to 320 metric tons, allowing the vessel to load and discharge heavy equipment without shoreside cranes. The addition follows the September reflagging of ARC Freedom , another nearly 8,000-car-capacity vessel brought into the U.S. fleet. ARC United joins sister ships ARC Freedom and ARC Commitment . According to the Seafarers International Union , ARC United replaces the retiring ARC Resolve in the Maritime Security Program, continuing ARC’s effort to modernize its U.S.-flag tonnage rather than increasing the number of vessels enrolled in the program. “In my 32 years at sea, my vessels moved a lot of military cargo, and I saw firsthand how much our troops depend on American civilian merchant mariners to keep them supplied,” said Captain Willie Barrere, national president of American Maritime Officers. ARC, part of the Wallenius Wilhelmsen group, is a major operator of U.S.-flag roll-on/roll-off vessels in international trade. The company also participates in the Voluntary Intermodal Sealift Agreement, which provides the U.S. military access to commercial shipping capacity and logistics networks during national emergencies. The two areas lie approximately 150 to 240 miles east of Pago Pago, in waters ranging from 4,630 to 20,100 feet deep. The $6 million in combined high bids matched the minimum asking price of $3 million for each area. Interior did not identify the winning bidders in its initial announcement. “This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said. The leases are intended to support exploration for minerals contained in polymetallic nodules and ferromanganese crusts, which can contain metals used in batteries, electronics, defense equipment and other industrial applications. The sale comes just three days after a federal judge in Hawaii ruled that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act in its review of the proposed lease sale. Despite that ruling, Interior proceeded with Thursday’s auction. Environmental group Oceana condemned the sale, warning that the move could open vast stretches of U.S. waters to commercial seabed mining. “The Trump administration has clearly put corporate interests above the health and well-being of our oceans,” said Julia Singer, Oceana’s defense campaign manager. “Mining in U.S. waters may begin off American Samoa, but make no mistake, it won’t stop there.” The lease areas are near the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a protected marine area that supports sea turtles, whales and other vulnerable species. Oceana said more than 76,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier stage of the leasing process, with the overwhelming majority opposing deep-sea mining. American Samoa Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula has also expressed opposition to commercial mineral extraction in the territory’s waters. The debate centers in part on the potential damage from mining the deep seabed, including disturbance of poorly understood habitats, sediment plumes and impacts on marine ecosystems. The administration argues that access to offshore critical minerals could strengthen U.S. manufacturing and national security while reducing reliance on foreign suppliers. Thursday’s auction does not authorize mining to begin. According to Interior, the leases would provide limited rights to conduct preliminary activities and an exclusive opportunity to submit plans for further exploration, testing and commercial extraction. Those activities would require additional environmental reviews and regulatory approvals. The leases carry a 20-year primary term, with royalties beginning at 2% of production value for the first five years of commercial production before increasing to 5%. The auction also comes as the administration pursues additional offshore mineral leasing proposals near the Northern Mariana Islands and in federal waters off Alaska and Virginia. For now, the American Samoa sale represents a historic step toward a domestic deep-sea mining industry, but one that faces significant hurdles before any commercial minerals are recovered. The existing wharf at Berths 148-149 would be used as a Marine Oil Terminal (MOT) while the new facilities at Berths 150-151 are being built. Landside facilities, including piping, vapor recovery systems, support systems, and tankage, would be modified and upgraded to support the new Berths 150-151 loading platform. The proposed project includes consideration of up to 40 years of continued operation as a MOT at Berths 148-151, currently proposed via a new 20-year entitlement with two optional 10-year extensions. articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: NAWC Import Growth at 17.6% in September
articles.summary: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. Following a sluggish start to the quarter, where laden imports contracted by ‑3.9% Y/Y in July and stabilized in August, September volumes surged to...
articles.body: In 2026‑Q3, North America West Coast (NAWC) ports experienced steady overall volume growth, driven almost entirely by a 17.6% Y/Y surge in laden imports in September. Following a sluggish start to the quarter, where laden imports contracted by ‑3.9% Y/Y in July and stabilized in August, September volumes surged to 1.45 million TEU. This double‑digit percentage growth in September is partially exaggerated by an unusually weak 2025‑Q3 baseline, when laden import growth dropped by ‑12.5 percentage points between July and September 2025. Still, 2026 marks the highest September laden import volume on record for the West Coast, eclipsing the previous high set in 2024. Overall, for 2026-Q3, NAWC ports recorded a 2.6% Y/Y increase in total container volume throughput, bringing the aggregate volume to 8.32 million TEU for the quarter. This growth was heavily weighted towards inbound cargo, with laden imports growing by 3.9% to reach 4.12 million TEU. In contrast, outbound cargo experienced more muted growth, as laden exports increased by just 1.8% to 1.21 million TEU, and empty container exports saw a smaller increase of 1.1% Y/Y to 2.67 million TEU. The operational impact of this highly compressed peak season has been substantial. Rather than managing a smoothed‑out influx of seasonal cargo, terminals were forced to handle an 11.3% M/M jump in laden imports from August to September, which is the highest M/M September increase across the 2012 to 2026 period. This level of sudden volatility creates acute stress on port infrastructure, chassis availability, and rail networks. As shippers navigated this, they overwhelmingly prioritized the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, which captured 73% of the West Coast’s total laden imports in 2026‑Q3.

articles.title: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4%
articles.summary: The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response…
articles.body: Middle East Conflict Could Cut Global Oil Demand by 4% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Yellow Boat The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday. Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that typically carries about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports. "In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran war," IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency's World Energy Outlook 2026. The conflict has resulted in cumulative losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said. The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz. Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. In that case, global oil demand in 2035 is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency's Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments' current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand. Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS. Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS. ELECTRIFICATION GROWING The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout. "Many countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, they decided to build energy at home," Birol said. Electricity's share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels. Alongside data centres, rising demand for cooling is emerging as one of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the first time, demand for cooling in buildings has exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use. articles.title: Constanta Port Grain Exports Rise by Double Digits in 2026
articles.summary: Grain exports through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta rose by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, the port authority said, helped by a good harvest, strong demand and Ukrainian exports passing through the port.The Constanta…
articles.body: Constanta Port Grain Exports Rise by Double Digits in 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 © Adobe Stock/dudlajzov Grain exports through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta rose by double digits in the first 10 months of the year, the port authority said, helped by a good harvest, strong demand and Ukrainian exports passing through the port. The Constanta port authority told Reuters the total volume of goods shipped through the port by end-October stood at 59.0 million tons, up 3.5% on the year. Grain exports through the port, one of the largest in the European Union, totaled 18.5 million tons, up 17.1% on the year. Ukrainian grain exports through Constanta jumped to 1.65 million tons compared with 321,000 tons in the first 10 months of 2025 as Kyiv sought alternative routes due to Russian attacks on its own seaports. The near five-year war between Russia and Ukraine has spilled over into the Black Sea, with some 15 merchant vessels hit over the past six weeks off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. Romania has said it is a target of Russia's hybrid war, which Moscow has repeatedly denied. The escalating maritime war off the coasts of European Union and NATO members Romania and Bulgaria is creating a major challenge for NATO, intelligence experts have said. The strikes focused mainly on ships headed to and from Romania's Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's largest grain exporters. Constanta has not been targeted despite the recent attacks. The port data does not include volumes handled through smaller Romanian ports and direct exports by rail and road. Romania is one of the EU's biggest grain exporters and Constanta also handles flows from landlocked neighbours including Serbia, Hungary and Moldova. To reflect rising Black Sea grain trade, Euronext said earlier this month it will launch Black Sea wheat and corn futures next year with physical delivery to the port of Constanta. "From an operational perspective Constanta does not have a problem; the grain terminals are moving well," Cezar Gheorghe of Romanian grain market consultancy AGRIColumn told Reuters. Gheorghe, who worked with Euronext to set up the futures service, said logistics costs had increased because of higher fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, as well as railroad bottlenecks because of Romanian infrastructure works and a shortage of locomotives. He said a good harvest in Romania, strong demand and relatively good sea transport costs for Constanta helped boost exports. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East.

(Screenshot from video) (Bloomberg) — Iran’s attacks on oil tankers crossing the crucial Strait of Hormuz are getting more intense, just as prices have tumbled due to a flood of supply from the Middle East. After a period of low-grade clashes, attacks increased in October and continued at the higher tempo this month, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In a sign of the mounting severity, at least two seafarers are missing after attacks this week. Traders and shipowners also circulated videos of a vessel engulfed in flames this week, though Bloomberg couldn’t immediately verify the footage. The flareups are happening as Brent crude futures slid about a fifth this month as Middle East exports approached pre-war levels, with the International Energy Agency last week saying that supply is outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. However, flows appear to have pulled back recently, though it’s not clear whether that’s due to intensifying attacks, with shipments often volatile from week to week and month to month. Critically, it’s also hard to quickly gauge how badly vessels are being hit as producers tend to remain tight-lipped due to security concerns. A key question is whether the attacks will be enough to meaningfully impact oil supply. “It seems like the new normal: Something like a war, but not exactly a war, with attacks on ships virtually every day,” said Georgios Sakellariou, an analyst at shipping-analytics platform Signal Ocean. “Oil is going out, but being certain about the volumes is complicated by the attacks and the secrecy.” Another issue is that while oil is flowing through Hormuz, more and more vessels will be needed as some are lost to attacks, he said. There are signs that attacks are becoming more serious. Several maritime security officials have said that Iran has attempted to hit the same ship on multiple occasions to deter salvors, and that there have also been sightings of limpet mines attached to vessels. One Gulf oil official said the situation in and around Hormuz had deteriorated since the US midterms. Gulf producers rely on energy exports to fund their economies. One senior Saudi shipping official said at a conference last week that the kingdom has no choice but to continue shipping oil through Hormuz, despite the attacks. Traders, analysts and shipping officials generally collate data from UK Maritime Trade Operations and the International Maritime Organization to assess the severity of attacks. But Gulf producers rarely release public information about attacks to help protect the security of vessels. So far this month, UKMTO has reported roughly one attack a day, with about 14 incidents occurring in Hormuz. Last month, it said it was struggling to accurately report the number of attacks as many companies weren’t reporting incidents to authorities. That’s fueling uncertainty about exactly how many attacks there are, as well as rampant rumors and speculation on vessels within commodity trading circles. While there’s also uncertainty about flows through Hormuz, there are signs that they have fallen from elevated levels this month, according to data from intelligence firms Kpler and Vortexa. The seven-day moving average of oil transits through Hormuz and net ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman eased to about 10 million barrels a day by Nov. 10, from around 13.4 million at the start of the month, Kpler data show. Recent data remain provisional as additional vessel crossings continue to be identified and validated. As producers boosted output last month, Saudi Arabia told the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries that the amount it actually supplied to the market was below its production. In the past, such a discrepancy has been an indication the kingdom was filling storage tanks or getting more out of Hormuz in advance of any escalation in the war. Both sides have lately stepped up tit-for-tat attacks in the ongoing war. US warplanes hit an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Persian Gulf this week, a response to Iran earlier targeting US personnel and assets. The chances of the US launching another round of mass strikes against Iran appear to have grown in recent days, according to Western officials, and the US issued a fresh warning to vessels breaching its blockade of Iranian ports this week. While the oil market has largely taken the recent flareups in its stride, that could change if attacks worsen. Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. said this week that one of its ships was hit when crossing Hormuz, that one seafarer was unaccounted for and a further 11 were injured. Kuwait has written to the IMO about attacks on eight of its tankers in recent weeks too. “Such actions undermine the security and stability of the region and constitute a clear breach of international law,” it said in a letter this week. “Kuwait reiterates its demands that the Islamic Republic of Iran immediately cease its unlawful attacks.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Enea Lebrun PANAMA CITY, Nov 18 (Reuters) – Panama’s comptroller general said on Wednesday it had filed a criminal complaint over suspected irregularities uncovered in an audit of a state contract with a unit of Hong Kong conglomerate CK Hutchison . The comptroller’s office said the complaint seeks an investigation into possible crimes linked to the port concession contract between the state and the CK Hutchison unit, Panama Ports Company (PPC). It said the filing covers former board members of the Panama Maritime Authority between 2014 and 2023, former administrators of the authority during that period, and PPC itself. The authority and PPC did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The complaint stems from findings in an audit of the company’s financial statements and compliance with contractual obligations, the comptroller said. The office did not detail the suspected irregularities, but said it had turned over documentation to the public prosecutor for investigation. The move marks the latest development in a broader dispute over PPC’s role operating the Balboa and Cristobal ports near the Panama Canal, one of the world’s busiest maritime waterways. Earlier this year, Panama moved to unwind the company’s port concessions, escalating a legal and diplomatic fight involving PPC and CK Hutchison. PPC has also accused Panamanian authorities in recent months of unlawfully seizing property and documents during the takeover of the facilities, allegations President Jose Raul Mulino has rejected. The dispute has complicated CK Hutchison’s proposed sale of a majority stake in its global ports business to a consortium led by BlackRock and Mediterranean Shipping Company. November 19, 2026 The S-band radar shown during acceptance testing in August 2026 at a site in Rio Grande do Sul. Photo: Climatempo The new Radar RS project implemented by StormGeo subsidiary Climatempo in the Brazilian State of Rio Grande do Sul is integrating radar technology with weather intelligence to turn atmospheric data into improved decision-making to safeguard lives and infrastructure. In 2024, Rio Grande do Sul experienced severe flooding that affected hundreds of municipalities, displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and caused significant loss of life and damage to infrastructure. As extreme weather events become more frequent and intense, the state is strengthening its meteorological monitoring and response capabilities to reduce risk, protect communities and build long‑term climate resilience. The Radar RS weather monitoring and intelligence system is designed to enhance monitoring capabilities and bolster emergency preparedness and response to protect citizens from extreme weather and flooding in one of Brazil’s most climate-vulnerable regions. Climatempo, a wholly-owned unit of StormGeo, is combining its local meteorological expertise with radar technology under the flagship project that comprises three S-band weather radars, data integration, and specialized meteorological and geological monitoring. Radar deployment entailed significant technical analysis of terrain, obstacles, access, safety, power, connectivity, radio-frequency interference, beam blockage and radar coverage to ensure optimal site selection. Nine sites were ranked as the highest-scoring locations – out of 32 coordinates initially studied – and organized into three geographic regions to support design of a three-radar network. Integrated radar solution The system integrates radar observations with satellites, lightning data, weather stations and meteorological models to provide a broader basis for analysis and interpretation. Integrated data can support real-time visualiation, storm-evolution tracking and very-short-range forecasting, helping to provide more context for monitoring and alerts. Climatempo’s team of meteorologists and data specialists use this integrated picture to provide continuous monitoring and operational decision support to the state’s civil defense and emergency management teams. Atmospheric signals can be turned into information to interpret weather, track its evolution, support alerts, and strengthen preparation and response to heavy rain, storms, strong winds and other extreme events. This can improve early warnings, emergency response and climate resilience for millions of residents in areas at risk. Mitigation of climate risk By combining robust infrastructure with local meteorological intelligence, the Radar RS system is expected to improve the accuracy and lead time of severe‑weather alerts, giving authorities more time to organize evacuations, protect critical assets and coordinate emergency response. Over time, the state aims to reduce the human, social and economic costs of flooding and other extreme events, while sharing learnings that can benefit other regions facing similar climate risks. The Radar RS project illustrates a broader shift in the role of weather information as continuous observation, multiple data sources, sophisticated interpretation, decision-support tools and integration into operational workflows become necessary to manage increasingly complex weather risks, with application across multiple sectors.

Photo: Hanwha Philly Shipyard Hanwha Philly Shipyard has begun construction of the first of four medium-range (MR) oil and chemical tankers for Hanwha Shipping, marking the start of a new U.S.-built tanker program as the South Korean conglomerate expands its American shipbuilding operations. The Philadelphia shipyard held a steel-cutting ceremony on November 17, kicking off a multiyear construction program with vessel deliveries scheduled between 2029 and 2030. The four tankers, each approximately 49,500 deadweight tons, will be designed to transport crude oil, refined petroleum products and chemicals. The vessels will be built to comply with the Jones Act, which requires vessels carrying cargo between U.S. ports to be American-built, American-owned and American-crewed. According to Hanwha Philly Shipyard , the tankers will feature energy-efficient designs and meet International Maritime Organization Type 2 and Type 3 chemical tanker standards. An optional Type II configuration with 18 segregations will allow the vessels to carry different cargoes separately. The program represents the first construction of an MR tanker in the United States in nearly a decade, according to Hanwha Shipping. “At a time when the domestic tanker fleet continues to age, these vessels will help modernize U.S. maritime transportation and enhance the resilience of America’s energy supply chain,” said James Sagar, CEO of Hanwha Shipping. The project also provides another source of work for the Philadelphia yard, which Hanwha acquired in December 2024 as part of its broader push into the U.S. maritime and defense markets. The shipyard is already building commercial containerships for Matson and completing the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program for the U.S. Maritime Administration. Hanwha Defense USA was also recently selected by TOTE Services to build a Medium Landing Ship for the U.S. Navy, expanding the yard’s work into naval shipbuilding . “A strong shipbuilding industry depends on consistent production, skilled people, and the ability to deliver quality vessels to our customers,” said Hyuk Kim, president of Hanwha Philly Shipyard. “This four-vessel program provides an important foundation for that work.” The tanker order strengthens Hanwha’s position in the domestic maritime market, adding new commercial construction work alongside its growing U.S. government shipbuilding portfolio. articles.summary: British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and...

(Image: UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch) British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and crew training that could put other large sailing yachts at risk. The recommendations, contained in the UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s (MAIB) final report released Thursday , follow the August 2024 disaster off Sicily that killed seven people, including British technology entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his daughter. While investigators found that Bayesian had an unrecognized vulnerability to extreme winds , the report goes further, identifying shortcomings in the regulatory framework governing large sailing yachts and recommending changes aimed at preventing similar accidents. At the center of the findings is a gap in the standards used to assess yacht stability. Neither the Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2), under which Bayesian was built, nor the subsequent Red Ensign Group Yacht Code required certain monohull sailing yachts to be assessed for the risk of being knocked onto their sides by high winds when operating without sails. Investigators found that the yacht’s towering mast and furled sails still generated substantial wind forces, even while the vessel was anchored. However, its approved stability information did not account for that risk, leaving the crew unaware of a potentially catastrophic vulnerability. The MAIB has recommended that the Red Ensign Group study the vulnerability of monohull sailing yachts certified under its Yacht Code and amend the regulations based on its findings. It also wants improved stability information and operational guidance for crews preparing for extreme weather, whether underway or at anchor. The investigation identified another significant safety concern involving lifesaving equipment. None of Bayesian ‘s liferafts automatically floated free and inflated when the yacht sank. Although their hydrostatic release units operated, the rafts remained trapped by their stowage arrangements. A crew member was forced to manually release one, allowing the 15 survivors to remain afloat until they were rescued. Investigators found that the liferaft arrangements met the regulatory requirements applicable when the yacht was originally surveyed. However, those standards did not adequately address what happens when a large sailing yacht is knocked onto its side. The MAIB is now recommending amendments to the Red Ensign Group Yacht Code requiring liferafts aboard sailing vessels vulnerable to knockdown to be capable of floating free, inflating and separating from the vessel as it sinks. The report also identified a separate deficiency in Bayesian ‘s original stability approval. Investigators determined that the yacht did not meet LY2’s minimum downflooding-angle requirement, leaving it vulnerable to progressive flooding at lower heel angles than the code permitted. The MAIB classified that finding as a safety issue that did not directly contribute to the accident. Beyond vessel design, investigators are calling for improvements in marine weather forecasting and professional training. Thunderstorms had been forecast near the yacht’s anchorage, but the available warnings did not adequately communicate the potential for destructive downbursts. Within just 14 minutes, relatively calm conditions gave way to winds of at least 68 knots, knocking the yacht onto its side in less than 15 seconds. The MAIB has recommended that the UK’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency review yacht officer training requirements to better address thunderstorms, downbursts and extreme wind gusts. It has also urged the Met Office to raise the treatment of rare but potentially catastrophic weather events with the World Meteorological Organization, while calling for updated guidance in Admiralty nautical publications. In a separate safety flyer issued to the yachting industry , the MAIB urged yacht owners, managers and crews to examine their vessels’ vulnerability to extreme weather and ensure their operating procedures adequately address the risks. “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised,” said Rob Loder, the UK’s Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents. Loder urged regulators, training providers and weather services to act on the investigation’s recommendations to prevent another tragedy. The proposed changes are not yet binding regulations. According to the final report, no safety actions had been taken by other organizations at the time of publication. The MAIB has also prepared a paper detailing the hazards identified in the investigation for consideration by the International Maritime Organization’s Sub-Committee on Implementation of IMO Instruments, potentially extending the safety discussion beyond the superyacht sector.
