articles.title: Crawling to the Rescue: Tiny Robots Built to Inspect Nuclear Waste Pipes
articles.summary: How do you inspect underground pipes that carry contaminated waste from the inside out? It’s a question the Hanford Site in Washington state has faced as it works to clean up the waste left by decades of nuclear production. With no easy solution…
articles.body: Crawling to the Rescue: Tiny Robots Built to Inspect Nuclear Waste Pipes Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 19, 2026 The robotics team at Sandia National Laboratories has built the SPIINE robot to inspect small pipes at the Department of Energy’s Hanford Site. Armed with LED lights, an onboard camera and a flexible body, it can easily drive through 90-degree turns and document its environment. (Photo by Craig Fritz) The robotics team at Sandia National Laboratories shows off an updated version of the SPIINE pipe crawler, designed to maneuver through and help inspect 2-inch pipes at the Hanford Site in Washington state. (Photo by Craig Fritz) How do you inspect underground pipes that carry contaminated waste from the inside out? It’s a question the Hanford Site in Washington state has faced as it works to clean up the waste left by decades of nuclear production. With no easy solution, Hanford turned to the Sandia National Laboratories and their tiny robot, who have come to the rescue. The Hanford Site pipe network Hanford is a decommissioned nuclear production complex managed by the Department of Energy. Located on the Columbia River, it was established in 1943 as part of the Manhattan Project and housed the world’s first full-scale plutonium production reactor. The Plutonium produced at the site was used in the first atomic bomb. What’s left at Hanford is radioactive waste that is housed in underground storage tanks, connected by a network of pipes. These pipes are designed to transfer waste from one tank to another, but the pipes are decades old and must be inspected to ensure they are in good condition. The pipes are hard to access–they're underground, run hundreds of feet in various directions, are double-walled and measure as little as two inches in diameter. Digging up these pipes for a visual inspection isn’t realistic or cost-effective. It also can’t ensure that pipes aren’t corroding from the inside out. While sending tiny cameras inside the pipes might seem like the obvious solution, earlier attempts had limited success. Traditional “push” cameras used for visual inspection could travel only about 10 feet at a time and were unable to maneuver tight 90-degree bends. The team also tried volumetric inspections using ultrasound, but the conventional probes are often too bulky to navigate through smaller pipes with tight bends. Tiny solution A Sandia team led by mechanical engineer Steve Buerger believes the solution is a tiny robot designed to propel itself through the pipes. “When we saw this need, we thought this is an area we can leverage some of those past works, do something unique, and really help with a very big problem,” Buerger said. “Sandia has made a lot of strides in making systems that are very small but still large enough to do real physical work.” Buerger and his team, which includes Daniel McArthur, Derya Tansel, Clint Hobart, and Josh Ortiz, came up with a robot called SPIINE, which stands for Self-Propelled Interior Inspector for Non-destructive-testing Examination. The robot is tiny in stature, measuring only two inches by six inches, but mighty in its abilities. It has a multi-axis body, adaptive wheels, steering capabilities and a high-resolution camera with adjustable LED lighting. Its motors are powerful enough to not only transport itself but carry a payload, such as an ultrasonic or electromagnetic field probe to measure pipe thickness. Operators control it with a standard video game controller “Our initial target is just being able to get eyes in the pipe,” McArthur said. “The goal is to be able to inspect for corrosion or other types of damage like cracks or anything that would raise a concern.” With few access points in the Hanford pipe network and hundreds of feet of pipe with multiple 90-degree turns to navigate, this robot had to do what other devices couldn’t. “We wanted a flexible body to let the pipe sort of guide the robot,” Buerger said. “It’s really designed to conform to those pipe walls, roll in the pipe and steer and re-orient itself if needed. It must handle a lot of things like T-joints and even making decisions on which way to go.” Years of work The SPIINE robot has undergone several updates and revisions since the project began more than two years ago. Getting it just right has not been easy. “One of the first challenges was tires. We’re using elastomeric or stretchy materials for things like the wheels,” Buerger said. “We had to do a lot of experimentation with different compounds to figure out what would interface best with pipe walls.” They also had to consider the tiny motors, and the big mission. “We had to figure out what would do best at transmitting power efficiently,” Buerger said. “Remember you have really limited forces from those small motors, the robot must be able to move itself along and pull payloads.” The robot must also overcome obstacles protruding from the pipe walls and navigate loose matter such as liquid sludge, or caked deposits. Then there are the hundreds of feet it must travel in one trip. SPIINE is designed to use a single cable that can transmit power and data to and from the robot while also bearing mechanical loads. It’s also designed to allow multiple robots or propulsion modules to be tied together in a series and additional payloads to be attached. “There was a strong sort of experimental piece there that went with this,” Buerger said. “We had to tackle the idea of being able to propel the robot at multiple points along the cable. When you’re dealing with very long distances and a cable in between with multiple bends, there’s something called the capstan effect where basically, the more bends you go around, the more you build up force required to drag a cable. With multiple bends, it gets really bad, really fast.” Think about a hose getting wrapped around a tree or another object. You pull, but the harder you pull, the more it tightens, requiring greater force to free it. If you have multiple robots propelling the cable between the wraps, you reduce that effect. Challenges ahead The next step is to test the robot in the real world. Tests at Sandia have been successful but seeing SPIINE at work at Hanford site could reveal new challenges. The team already knows of some issues it will have to tackle, including developing a self-cleaning function that would enable the robot to wipe its camera lens or a clean dirty pipe wall. The team is also working on a built-in, fail-safe recovery system in case the robot becomes stuck or disabled. Researchers are also exploring the idea of designing microscale ultrasonic sensors that would fit on the robot because conventional sensors don’t fit through a 90-degree turn. For the team, this is an important project to perfect. “We are helping to keep the environment clean, so it’s the mission that is really satisfying,” Buerger said. “One of the most rewarding parts of being a robotics engineer is using technology to help keep people out of harm’s way. SPIINE is a great example of that,” McArthur said. “The US Department of Energy’s Office of Environmental Management face an enormous challenge in addressing the environmental legacy from decades of nuclear weapons development and government-sponsored nuclear energy research. If our work can help inform critical inspections, reduce uncertainty, and minimize risk to workers, then we are contributing to something much larger than the robot itself. That is the kind of impact that makes this work so fulfilling.”

articles.summary: London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia.
articles.body: Business & Finance November 19, 2026 · 6 minutes ago $960 million deal enabling NEO NEXT+ to bring EnQuest’s UK North Sea business into its fold London Stock Exchange-listed energy firm EnQuest has decided to exit the UK upstream arena to strengthen its focus on Southeast Asia. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Magnus platform Source: EnQuest UK’s independent oil and gas producer NEO NEXT+ Energy is boosting its portfolio with the acquisition of EnQuest’s UK upstream business and associated infrastructure, as the seller accelerates its pivot toward Southeast Asia, following a series of acquisitions in Malaysia. EnQuest has entered into an agreement to sell its UK upstream business and associated infrastructure through the sale of EnQuest Britain to NEO NEXT+ Energy for total consideration of up to $960 million, encompassing $840 million in upfront cash consideration to be paid on completion, subject to customary closing adjustments, including working capital, together with up to $120 million contingent cash consideration. The proposed disposal is based on an economic effective date of January 1, 2027, and is subject to customary conditions, including, among others, regulatory approvals and completion of the firm’s acquisitions of participating interests in four PSCs in Malaysia, which remain on track to complete on December 31, 2026. These moves continue EnQuest’s strategic pivot to Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, creating a low-cost, highly resilient platform from which to pursue further near-term capital-efficient organic and inorganic growth. Following completion of the proposed disposal, EnQuest intends to repay debt drawn in connection with the proposed acquisitions, while retaining significant liquidity and financial flexibility to pursue material organic growth and further acquisition opportunities across the region. Related Articles Fossil Energy EnQuest makes $833 million play to expand its Southeast Asian oil & gas arsenal 3 min read " The resulting business will have a materially lower cost base and significantly enhanced balance sheet strength to pursue both organic investment and further value-accretive acquisitions across Southeast Asia, while supporting sustainable shareholder returns. We are immensely proud of what our teams have achieved in the UK and believe that NEO NEXT+’s combination of scale and track record as a leading North Sea operator, and diverse asset portfolio will enhance career opportunities for our people. We are committed to working closely with NEO NEXT+, our employees, joint venture partners and other stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition. " — Amjad Bseisu Chief Executive Officer of EnQuest The company’s board of directors believes the proposed disposal represents a significant step forward in the continued strategic evolution of EnQuest, crystallizing material value from the firm’s UK upstream portfolio, significantly strengthening its capital structure and completing the repositioning toward Southeast Asia. EnQuest took these steps to establish Southeast Asia as its primary operating region, where it sees significant opportunities for further high-return, capital-efficient growth, and maintain its established focus on operatorship and highly tangible reserves, deploying its operating capabilities and experienced asset teams to enhance value via a number of measures, including recovery factor improvement and conversion of 2C resources. In addition, the company believes this divestment and recent acquisitions provide a strengthened platform from which to accelerate further organic growth initiatives in Southeast Asia and capitalize on further inorganic growth opportunities across the region. The remaining EnQuest portfolio on a 2025 net participating interest basis, following completion of the proposed disposal and the acquisitions, is expected to benefit from around 70,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) in the Southeast Asia business, with a unit opex of about $11/boe, a reduction of approximately 57% against its 2025 unit opex of $25/boe, generating a pro forma EBITDA of circa $500 million. While elaborating that production has grown further via the addition of low-cost Seligi 1b gas volumes in 2026, the firm emphasizes the substantial capital-efficient growth potential, including opportunities to leverage existing infrastructure, adding that its Southeast Asia capital investment is focused on high-return production enhancement activity, with minimal infrastructure investment required. The proposed disposal will involve the sale of all of the issued shares of EnQuest Britain, which through its subsidiaries holds the firm’s UK upstream assets, including Magnus , Kraken , and the Greater Kittiwake Area (operated), Golden Eagle (non-operated), and the undeveloped Bressay field and Bentley discovery. Additionally, the portfolio entails UK decommissioning and midstream assets, including EnQuest’s operating interest in the Sullom Voe Terminal , the Northern Leg Gas Pipeline , and the Ninian Pipeline system. Employees supporting these operations will transfer to the new owner as a result of the deal. EnQuest’s UK upstream assets contributed 31,122 boe/d of average net production (92% liquids and 8% gas) for the year ended December 31, 2025, when the portfolio comprised approximately 122 million boe of 2P reserves and 308 million boe of 2C resources. " The proposed disposal represents a significant repositioning of EnQuest, continuing the company’s transformation from a UK-focused operator into a business focused on high-quality assets in Southeast Asia, underpinned by a simple, strong capital structure. Following completion of both the proposed acquisitions and the proposed disposal, EnQuest will be a significant operator of scale, with its upstream portfolio focused solely on its 97% operated 2P asset base in Southeast Asia. " — EnQuest underlined. The completion of the divestment is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to conditions set out in the agreement, such as receipt of applicable regulatory approvals, including NSTA and NSIA approval and CMA clearance; completion of the company’s previously announced proposed acquisitions of participating interests offshore Malaysia; and other customary approvals and consents, including, amongst others, RBL lender consent and replacement of UK Decommissioning Security Agreements. Upon completion of the disposal, EnQuest will have interests in production, development, and exploration assets in Malaysia, Vietnam, Brunei, and Indonesia, as well as Veri Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary, and associated CCUS interests, which sit outside this perimeter. articles.body: Collaboration November 19, 2026 · 1 minute ago Wison and DNV shake hands on enhancing global energy project delivery This strategic pact is set on strengthening energy project delivery, boosting quality, and managing risks across global projects. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Cap Jiangjun Wang, Country Manager, Greater China, Industrial Services at DNV, and Lv Jianning, VP, Wison Engineering, signed the agreement in the presence of Mohamed Houari, CEO, Industrial Services at DNV, and Zhou Hongliang, CEO, Wison Engineering. Source: DNV Norway’s assurance and risk management company DNV and China’s Wison Engineering have forged a partnership to combine their engineering, project delivery, and technical assurance expertise in a bid to improve quality, manage risks, and support increasingly complex energy projects worldwide. The two companies have signed a strategic cooperation agreement, pairing Wison’s engineering and project delivery capabilities with DNV’s technical assurance expertise, with the aim of bolstering quality, managing risk, and building confidence across energy projects worldwide. This agreement establishes a framework for long-term cooperation across engineering project support, independent inspection, and supplier quality management, while exploring opportunities in areas including hydrogen, ammonia, carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS), and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). " The energy industry is changing rapidly, and delivering the next generation of projects requires confidence in technology, quality, supply chains and execution. By combining Wison’s strong engineering and project delivery capabilities with DNV’s independent assurance and risk management expertise, we can help manage complexity and move projects forward with greater confidence. " — Mohamed Houari Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Industrial Services at DNV With the energy transition accelerating and projects becoming increasingly complex, the duo’s collaboration intends to combine Wison Engineering’s engineering and EPC capabilities with DNV’s independent technical assurance and risk management expertise to fortify quality, manage project risks, and augment confidence throughout project delivery. The European and Chinese duo will also explore cooperation around global supply-chain quality, including supplier assessments, audits, capability building, and data-led approaches to quality improvement. DNV and Wison Engineering plan to focus on turning this agreement into concrete projects and initiatives. " This cooperation creates an opportunity to bring together the complementary strengths of Wison and DNV as we expand our support for customers globally. We see significant potential to collaborate across both conventional and emerging energy sectors, particularly in areas such as hydrogen, ammonia, CCUS and sustainable aviation fuels. " — Zhou Hongliang CEO of Wison Engineering DNV signed up to acquire WellSpot from Equinor earlier this year, bringing well data, analysis, and standardized workflows into one place, so operators can track and manage accumulated fatigue damage throughout the life of a subsea well. articles.title: Red Sea returns are rewriting carrier reliability, not just transit times
articles.summary: The return of container services to the Red Sea is changing Asia–Europe schedules again. For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope. The harder question is whether the shorter passage will produce more dependable arrival windows. The...
articles.body: The return of container services to the Red Sea is changing Asia–Europe schedules again. For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope. The harder question is whether the shorter passage will produce more dependable arrival windows. The transition is taking place service by service. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd moved their joint ME1 service, linking India and Europe, to the trans-Suez route from November, with the first westbound and eastbound sailings scheduled from Salalah on 4 November and Tangier on 13 November. On 17 November, Hapag-Lloyd announced that three further Gemini services, NE1, NE2 and NE3, would also return to Suez, with initial westbound transitions scheduled for December 2026 and January 2027. The sequence shows that the return is being managed through individual service decisions, not a single network-wide switch. For cargo owners, this distinction matters. A shorter sea passage changes the planned transit time. It does not, by itself, confirm that a vessel will arrive on schedule, that a transshipment connection will hold or that cargo will be available when expected. A Shorter Route Does Not Guarantee a Reliable Schedule Cape diversions extended Asia–Europe rotations and absorbed vessel capacity. Returning to Suez can release sailing days and help carriers redesign rotations. But the timetable also depends on port calls, vessel deployment, buffer time, terminal congestion, transshipment connections and the recovery of equipment flows. The Red Sea return is therefore unfolding against a wider reliability problem. Xeneta’s October 2026 Schedule Reliability Scorecard put global on-time arrivals at 24%, the lowest monthly average since July 2022. On the Far East–Europe trade, only 7% of vessels arrived on time, while average delay reached 9.0 days. The scorecard also found that Gemini services recorded 7% on-time arrivals on this lane, compared with 23% for non-alliance services. Gemini’s average delay was 9.4 days, against 6.8 days for Ocean Alliance and 7.8 days for MSC. These figures should not be read as evidence that the Suez return caused the delays. Xeneta points to broader pressures, including disruption at Asian ports, the effects of typhoons, vessel queues and changes in blank sailings. They do, however, show why shippers should avoid treating a shorter route as a proxy for better schedule performance. Reliability Is Specific to the Service and Direction A carrier’s network-wide reliability score can conceal substantial differences between individual services, port pairs and voyage directions. A service may use Suez on its westbound leg while retaining a Cape diversion eastbound. Another may return to the canal only after a particular sailing date. The service name alone is not enough to establish how a booked container will move. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s November changes illustrate this staged approach. The ME1 service has moved to Suez, while the NE1, NE2 and NE3 transitions are scheduled across different weeks from December into January. The carriers have said the planned dates remain subject to operational conditions. Their updates also make clear that further routing changes depend on the security situation. That qualification remains material. The Norwegian Maritime Authority’s October 30 notice kept ISPS Security Level 3 in force in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for Norwegian vessels, with Level 2 applying in the southern Red Sea and northern Gulf of Aden. A carrier may therefore retain alternative routing options even after a service has returned to the shorter corridor. For a shipper, the relevant comparison is not simply which carrier has announced a Suez return. It is which specific service is scheduled to use the route, in which direction, from which voyage, and what contingency applies if the plan changes. What Shippers Should Test Before 2027 Contracts Reliability should be assessed through a consistent set of service-level measures rather than a carrier’s headline transit-time promise. Before committing cargo volumes, shippers and forwarders should examine: On-time performance by port pair and direction: Request a rolling 12-month record for the actual service and trade lane, not only a global carrier or alliance average. Delay severity: Compare average and median delay, and examine how often arrivals exceed the agreed delivery window. A high on-time percentage can still hide a small number of severe delays. Blank sailings and port omissions: Review cancellations, skipped calls, schedule revisions and changes to transshipment hubs. These can disrupt cargo plans even when the sailing that operates arrives on time. Routing and contingency terms: Confirm whether the carrier can switch between Suez and the Cape, how notice will be provided, and how additional transit time, surcharges or revised port rotations will be handled. End-to-end cargo availability: Track the time from vessel arrival to discharge, release and onward movement. A timely arrival does not guarantee that cargo will be ready for collection or connected to inland transport. The last point is important because the vessel schedule is only one part of the logistics chain. Vyansa Intelligence’s Global Captive Logistics Market Report estimates that transportation services account for around 40% of the global captive logistics market’s service-type segment. The report includes seaways and inland waterways within its transportation-mode coverage. This is not a measure of ocean-carrier reliability, but it illustrates the weight of transport execution within wider logistics networks, where vessel delays can affect inventory, warehouse slots and onward distribution. Shippers should also compare reliability data using the same provider and methodology across carriers. Schedule reliability datasets do not always use identical coverage or calculation rules, so combining scores from different providers can create misleading rankings. The most useful tender evidence is a like-for-like comparison of the service, direction, port pair and reporting period that the cargo will actually use. A 2027 Decision Based on Performance, Not the Map The return to Suez can shorten voyages and improve vessel utilisation, but those benefits will be realised unevenly as carriers adjust rotations and retain contingency options. Reliability will depend on how consistently each service operates through the transition, how quickly downstream port and equipment flows adapt, and whether security conditions allow the new routing to continue. For 2027 contracts, shippers should treat the announced route as one input, not the final verdict. The stronger choice will be the service that can demonstrate stable port rotations, controlled delays, transparent contingency arrangements and dependable cargo availability across the full journey. Shammi Thakur is the Research Director at Vyansa Intelligence, with over 15 years of experience in market research, strategic intelligence and industry analysis. His work includes maritime and logistics research, tracking industry developments, operational trends and the factors shaping shipping and supply chain decisions.

articles.body: Decommissioning November 19, 2026 · 1 minute ago Boskalis Subsea Services joins one of 'UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programs' NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Boskalis Subsea Services via LinkedIn Boskalis Subsea Services has secured a long-term contract with Apache North Sea for what is described as one of the UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programs. Boskalis Subsea Services will deliver a comprehensive subsea decommissioning program covering subsea wells, subsea structures and associated pipelines and infrastructure, including the flushing, disconnection, recovery and disposal of all subsea infrastructure for the operator’s Forties and Beryl fields in the UK North Sea. “This contract marks another significant milestone as we continue to progress one of the UK’s largest offshore decommissioning programmes. As our Forties and Beryl assets move through the next stage of their lifecycle, we remain focused on delivering decommissioning safely, responsibly and efficiently, while drawing on the expertise of experienced partners to help achieve that," said Donald Martin , Vice President of Decommissioning at Apache. "Boskalis demonstrated the technical capability, collaborative approach and long-term commitment we were looking for throughout the tender process. By working together as one integrated team, we are building the foundations for a programme that will deliver value over the coming decade and support the responsible retirement of this significant North Sea infrastructure.” The company plans to establish a dedicated core team within Apache’s Aberdeen office, working closely with Apache personnel to support planning, engineering and project delivery. According to the firm, a predominantly ROV-led approach will be used across much of the campaign. “As the North Sea continues to evolve, decommissioning will play an increasingly important role in supporting the basin’s future. This programme draws on the full breadth of our subsea capability, combining engineering expertise, offshore execution, advanced ROV systems, remote operations and diving services to deliver safe and efficient outcomes for our clients," said Stuart Cameron , Managing Director of Boskalis Subsea Services. "We have invested significantly in developing these capabilities over recent years, and this award reflects the growing demand for integrated subsea solutions that can support large-scale decommissioning programmes from planning through to execution.” Related Articles News Boskalis Subsea Services wins its first decommissioning-specific contract with Shell 1 min read Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: Napier Port lifts earnings despite flat container volumes
articles.summary: Napier Port reported further earnings growth for the financial year ended 30 September 2026, supported by a stronger cargo mix, higher container revenue and its yield-management strategy. Revenue increased by 11.7% to NZ$176.2 million, compared with NZ$157.7 million in the previous financial year. Reported net profit...
articles.body: Napier Port reported further earnings growth for the financial year ended 30 September 2026, supported by a stronger cargo mix, higher container revenue and its yield-management strategy. Revenue increased by 11.7% to NZ$176.2 million, compared with NZ$157.7 million in the previous financial year. Reported net profit after tax rose by 15% to NZ$35.5 million. Underlying net profit increased by 30.5% to NZ$36.9 million. The port’s result from operating activities reached NZ$75.7 million, representing an increase of 17.9%. Its operating margin improved from 40.7% to 43%. “2026 was a strong year of service delivery and continued earnings growth for Napier Port,” said Blair O’Keeffe, Chair of Napier Port. “The result reflects the strength of our diverse cargo base, continued progress with our yield and cost management strategies, and the resilience of Hawke’s Bay’s primary sector,” he added. Container throughput remains at 250,000 TEU Container volumes remained unchanged at approximately 250,000 TEU. Full container volumes increased by 5%, supported by higher exports of apples, meat and timber and increased imports of paper products and fertiliser. Empty and other container movements declined by 5.6%, primarily because of lower transshipment activity. Average container services revenue per TEU increased by 18.9%. Napier Port attributed the rise to a higher-yielding cargo mix, tariff and levy adjustments, increased vessel-call revenue and growth at its Viewpoint supply-chain business. Viewpoint recorded higher volumes during the year as more customers outside the region moved cargo through Napier Port. Much of this cargo travelled by rail between Napier and Palmerston North. Bulk cargo volumes decreased by 2.7% to 3.32 million tonnes. Log exports fell by 2.8% to 2.6 million tonnes, while bulk imports declined by 7.2%. Cruise calls decreased from 78 to 55 and generated NZ$6.5 million in revenue, down 20.8% from the previous year. Autonomous terminal operations planned for 2027 Napier Port continued its three-year investment programme during the financial year. Its ShoreTension mooring system entered operation at 6 Wharf, while the new dredger KAPUKA was launched. The port’s container terminal transformation project also moved into operational testing. Napier Port has activated its private 5G network and is testing its first battery-electric truck. It plans to introduce autonomous truck-and-trailer operations at the container terminal during 2027. The company is also assessing future container crane replacements, with a final investment decision expected during the 2027 financial year. Napier Port expects an underlying result from operating activities of between NZ$80 million and NZ$85 million in FY2027, assuming current market conditions continue.

REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo By Yongchang Chin Nov 19, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Some of the world’s top commodity-trading houses are in talks to secure more long-term supplies of Qatari crude, seeking to build on their success at shuttling oil out of the Persian Gulf during the Iran-US war. The companies spoke with state-owned QatarEnergy this month to ask for volumes to be supplied over 2027, according to people involved in the discussions. Grades of interest centered on Qatar Marine and Land varieties, they said, asking not to be named as the talks are private. Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up in recent months, despite the stalemate between Washington and Tehran and continued attacks on vessels. The flows have helped to drag prices lower, with traders proving adept at moving volumes and shouldering the risks, while some refiners have been more wary. That’s opening up opportunities for 2027. Qatar — which also provided almost a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas before the war damaged infrastructure and hampered shipments — is a located within the Persian Gulf, and its shipments must transit Hormuz. Term deals allow for contracted volumes to be supplied over longer periods, handing the supplier and buyer more certainty than relying on spot shipments. With a little more than a month left before 2027 contracts start in January, several Asian refiners and traders are still in talks with producers like QatarEnergy and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. Adnoc has also been willing to sell more term supplies to trading companies next year, Bloomberg has reported. QatarEnergy typically inks yearlong supply deals with refiners, but such discussions for next year’s term volumes have been slowed down by issues surrounding shipping crude through Hormuz, the people said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Some traders already buy Qatari crude on a term basis, but the volumes have mainly centered on the flagship Al-Shaheen grade. Others typically secure cargoes via monthly tenders, a regular fixture before the Iran war, and one which QatarEnergy has pushed to reinstate. During the conflict, commodity houses — including Vitol Group, Mercuria Energy Group and Trafigura Group, as well as the arms of producers such as TotalEnergies SE and Adnoc — have assumed greater prominence in ensuring the continuity of energy flows between the Persian Gulf and Asia. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The crew of British tech tycoon Mike Lynch's yacht, which sank off Sicily in 2024 killing him and six others, was unaware of its vulnerability to strong winds because the risk had never been assessed, a British investigation found on Thursday.

REUTERS/Danilo Arnone TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY By Paul Sandle LONDON, Nov 19 (Reuters) – The crew of British tech tycoon Mike Lynch’s yacht, which sank off Sicily in 2024 killing him and six others, was unaware of its vulnerability to strong winds because the risk had never been assessed, a British investigation found on Thursday. The 56-meter-long (184-foot) Bayesian was moored off Porticello, near Palermo, in August 2024 when it was hit by a violent downburst in a storm, forcing it onto its side, where it began taking on water. Unable to right itself, the yacht flooded, capsized and sank around 18 minutes later, Britain’s Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) said. Lynch, a British tech entrepreneur , had been celebrating his acquittal on 15 counts of fraud two months earlier over the sale of his company Autonomy to Hewlett Packard. He was sailing with his family and friends who supported him during the US trial. His 18-year-old daughter Hannah died, along with lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife Judy, and chef Recaldo Thomas. The yacht was vulnerable to violent winds and was probably knocked over by gusts of more than 117 kilometers (73 miles) per hour, British investigators said in 2025. Thursday’s report by the MAIB, which was not designed to determine liability, said the yacht’s vulnerability to wind when operating under engine power had never been assessed, leaving its 10-person crew unaware of a critical risk. Its 72-meter mast and furled sails contributed significantly to the risk, the report said. The yacht’s stability information book did not identify its vulnerabilities when anchored with its sails furled and keel raised, meaning neither the owner nor crew knew of the danger. “The vulnerability of Bayesian to wind heeling moments while in the motoring condition had never been assessed, resulting in the crew being unaware of a critical risk to the vessel and unable to take account of it in their operations,” it said. The report said the safety of the six guests and nine crew members who escaped the yacht and were rescued relied heavily on the training, experience and initiative of individual crew members. The Bayesian was built in 2008 by Perini Navi, an Italian luxury yacht maker owned by the Italian Sea Group. The company in 2024 said the sinking was due to a chain of human errors, and if the crew had shut all doors and hatches, turned on the engine, lifted the anchor, lowered the keel and turned the yacht to face the wind, it would have suffered no damage. articles.body: International consultancy Steer has completed the acquisition of Mercator International, expanding its advisory capabilities in the ports, maritime and freight sectors. Based in Kirkland, Washington, Mercator advises port authorities, terminal operators, shipping lines, logistics companies and investors on commercial strategy and infrastructure transactions. The acquisition strengthens Steer’s presence in North America while expanding its expertise in maritime infrastructure and investment advisory. Mercator will become part of Steer’s North America division, led by Herb Higginbotham. However, the company will continue operating under its existing name, maintaining its current projects and customer relationships. Acquisition expands maritime advisory capabilities Founded in 2000, Mercator has completed more than 150 commercial due diligence projects. It has also advised over 40 investors and financial institutions on transactions worldwide. Its previous assignments include advising the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma on the formation of the Northwest Seaport Alliance. The company has also supported the Quebec Port Authority on a new container terminal project and advised the Macquarie-led consortium on its acquisition of Long Beach Container Terminal. Through the acquisition, Steer will combine Mercator’s maritime expertise with its wider capabilities in rail, freight, infrastructure planning and investment advisory. “Mercator brings an excellent team of ports and maritime experts that will strengthen our offer well beyond North America,” said Hugh Jones, CEO, Steer. “As our second acquisition this year, it’s a clear signal of where Steer is heading as we deliver on our ambitious growth plans,” Jones added. The transaction marks Steer’s fourth acquisition since 2021. Its previous acquisitions include Fourth Economy in the United States, alongside Amberside Advisors and Evolution Infrastructure in the United Kingdom. Mercator will also work closely with Steer’s existing ports and maritime practice, led by Alberto Preti in Italy and Steve Wray in the United Kingdom. Steve Rothberg, founder of Mercator International, said the combination would allow the company to offer clients a broader range of services while maintaining its established approach to maritime advisory. The financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

articles.title: Torm hits back at Hafnia over rejected merger bids
articles.summary: Danish product tanker giant Torm has hit back at Hafnia following its abandoned takeover pursuit, revealing that it rejected several merger proposals from its rival because they offered no meaningful premium and substantially undervalued the company. The Jacob Meldgaard-led owner broke its silence after BW...
articles.body: Europe Tankers Torm hits back at Hafnia over rejected merger bids Adis Ajdin November 19, 2026 0 668 2 minutes read Torm Torm Danish product tanker giant Torm has hit back at Hafnia following its abandoned takeover pursuit, revealing that it rejected several merger proposals from its rival because they offered no meaningful premium and substantially undervalued the company. The Jacob Meldgaard-led owner broke its silence after BW Group-backed Hafnia announced plans to exit its near-20% stake, bringing an end to its attempts to combine two of the world’s largest product tanker operators. Torm confirmed that Hafnia had submitted a number of conditional, all-share proposals, but said none offered an effective premium for control. Its board, following discussions with financial and legal advisers, unanimously rejected each proposal and informed Hafnia of its decision on every occasion. Torm chairman Simon Mackenzie Smith defended the decision, arguing that Hafnia had failed to recognise the company’s operating performance and future prospects. “The proposals from Hafnia fundamentally failed to recognize that track record and the significant future value embedded in the One Torm platform,” he said. The response comes after Hafnia chief executive Søren Steenberg Jensen announced that the company was walking away from its consolidation ambitions, having failed to secure Torm’s support. Jensen said the company’s approaches had not been reciprocated and that continued resistance would undermine the potential benefits of bringing the two tanker groups together. Torm’s response makes clear that the disagreement was not over whether proposals had been received, but over their valuation and the absence of a meaningful takeover premium. The Danish owner did not disclose the proposed exchange ratios or other financial terms of Hafnia’s approaches. Hafnia, which spent more than $500m building its position in Torm, now intends to dispose of its entire holding of approximately 20.36m shares, representing around 19.8% of the company. The stake was valued at $686.6m based on Torm’s November 17 closing share price. Hafnia’s preferred route is to distribute the shares directly to its own shareholders through a special dividend, giving them the option of retaining or selling their individual holdings. The proposal remains subject to third-party cooperation, with Hafnia setting November 25 as the deadline for determining whether the distribution can proceed. If the necessary arrangements cannot be completed, Hafnia plans to pay a regular cash dividend under its existing policy and consider alternative ways to exit its Torm investment. articles.title: Europe and Central Asia are closing the distance. Growing trade needs efficient logistics
articles.summary: The economies of Central Asia grew by a combined total of more than 6% in 2025, according to estimates by the World Bank and the Eurasian Development Bank. This growth is increasingly visible both in trade volumes and in expanding transport options. This November marks three years since SUUS established its presence...
articles.body: The economies of Central Asia grew by a combined total of more than 6% in 2025, according to estimates by the World Bank and the Eurasian Development Bank. This growth is increasingly visible both in trade volumes and in expanding transport options. This November marks three years since SUUS established its presence in Almaty, and for the past six months we have also been operating in Tashkent. This time has given us an even better understanding of the region and confirmed our view that it is an attractive direction for growth, both for Polish companies and for other global players. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are the two largest economies in Central Asia and the pillars of its development. Uzbekistan closed 2025 with GDP growth of 7.7%, according to the National Statistics Committee, and Kazakhstan with 6.5%, according to preliminary data from the Bureau of National Statistics. In both countries, logistics grew faster than the economy as a whole. In Uzbekistan, the value of transport services rose by 10.8%, while in Kazakhstan the transport and warehousing sector expanded by 20.4%, more than three times faster than GDP. From our perspective, these are the figures that matter most. They show that rising demand is already translating into real flows of goods and the development of the transport and logistics sector. Trade with the European Union is growing in both directions In 2024, Poland exported goods worth EUR 1.6 billion to Central Asia, EUR 0.6 billion more than in 2021. Two-thirds of these exports go to Kazakhstan, according to a report by the Polish Economic Institute (PIE). Polish and European companies from the household appliances, construction, fashion and pharmaceutical sectors increasingly treat Central Asia as a target market. These are precisely the industries we work with on this route, handling their shipments to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Trade is also supported by institutions and carriers. The Polish Investment and Trade Agency (PAIH) has an office in Astana and is accelerating the opening of a representative office in Tashkent, while since May LOT Polish Airlines has been flying to Almaty, its third destination in the region after Astana and Tashkent. The flow in the opposite direction is just as clear. According to the European Commission, the EU accounts for nearly a third of Central Asia’s exports and is its main export market. The region delivers to the EU mainly oil, gas, metals, and cotton fibre. Since 2021, Uzbekistan has benefited from the EU’s GSP+ trade preferences, and in October 2025 it signed an Enhanced Partnership and Cooperation Agreement with the EU. For Central Asian exporters, Central and Eastern Europe, including Poland, is a natural gateway to the EU market. The region is accelerating investment in roads and rail Kazakhstan is preparing the largest infrastructure programme in its history. By 2029, the country plans to invest more than USD 14 billion in projects covering roads, railways, airports and energy, among others. The effects of earlier investments are already visible. According to Kazakhstan’s Minister of Transport, 94% of national roads meet the required quality standards, which translates into shorter and more predictable journey times. At the same time, countries in the region are expanding their networks for international freight. The Bakhty–Ayagoz line, with a third rail border crossing to China, is due to be completed by 2027. Closest to completion is the Darbaza–Maktaaral line in southern Kazakhstan, near the border with Uzbekistan, where traffic is set to start by the end of this year. The line will relieve the key route via Saryagash station to Tashkent. This matters for growing trade, as rail freight between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan rose by 16% in 2025. The new airport in Tashkent is being developed by Uzbekistan together with investors from Saudi Arabia, Japan and South Korea, a sign that companies from the world’s leading economies are committing to these markets for the long term. The Middle Corridor, the route from China through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to Central and Eastern Europe, is becoming increasingly important for transport between Asia and Europe. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, volumes on this route grew from 0.8 to 4.5 million tonnes per year over seven years. Infrastructure is being developed as well: a new container hub has opened in the port of Aktau, and the expansion of the Dostyk–Moyynty rail line is set to increase its capacity fivefold. Meanwhile, a new berth is under construction at the Georgian port of Poti, which will ultimately raise its capacity to 3 million tonnes. In its October report on the Middle Corridor, the World Bank points out that the route’s potential will depend not only on infrastructure investment, but also on shorter waiting times at borders and simpler documentation. Cargo changes transport mode several times along the way and passes through numerous transshipments, while strong winds at the port of Aktau and winter snowfall continue to reduce operational efficiency. For companies using this route, transit time and efficient customs clearance remain critical. The advantage therefore goes to an operator that knows local conditions, plans the entire supply chain and takes responsibility for every transshipment. Successful expansion starts with a local partner Foreign investors in Central Asia need local know-how above all else. European companies entering Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are looking for a partner who understands local realities: business culture, market regulations, customs procedures, and settlements in local currency. Businesses from Central Asia targeting customers in Europe, in turn, need a logistics operator present in EU countries. At SUUS, we bring these two perspectives together. At our branches in Almaty and Tashkent, we provide road, rail, air and sea freight, intermodal solutions, warehousing, and customs services. Having our own structures in Central Asia means that solutions are designed by local teams who know the market and its conditions. The advantage in the region will go to operators that are present on both sides of the corridor and operate efficiently in all of its markets. Today, we are transferring three years of experience from Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan. For us, both markets are part of a single CEECA bridge linking China, Central Asia and Central and Eastern Europe. We look to the coming years with great optimism: if investments in rail and airports are delivered on schedule and border procedures are simplified, trade between Europe and Central Asia will have room to grow even faster. Andrzej Kozłowski, Member of the Management Board, Rohlig SUUS Logistics

articles.body: Fincantieri’s subsidiary WASS Submarine Systems has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with India’s Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) to explore cooperation in underwater defence systems. The agreement was signed during the Defence Industrial Cooperation Dialogue in New Delhi. It establishes a framework for potential industrial collaboration involving heavyweight torpedoes and torpedo countermeasure systems. The two companies will examine opportunities to develop manufacturing and technical support capabilities in India. Agreement targets local production and technical support The proposed cooperation covers several stages of underwater defence system production. These include component manufacturing, energetic sections, subassemblies, final assembly and factory testing. The companies will also explore maintenance and in-service support activities, allowing potential cooperation to extend beyond initial production. Under the agreement, WASS will contribute its experience in underwater defence technology, while BDL will provide its established industrial capabilities in India. The partnership aims to strengthen local manufacturing expertise and support India’s long-term development of domestic underwater defence capabilities. For Fincantieri, the agreement represents another step in expanding its industrial relationships in the Indian market. WASS previously secured a contract to supply torpedoes to the Indian Navy, strengthening its position in the country’s naval defence sector. The latest agreement builds on that presence by examining opportunities for broader industrial cooperation. However, the MoU does not constitute a confirmed manufacturing contract. The companies have not disclosed an investment value, production volumes or an implementation timetable.
